instruction: Independently compare the original and rewrite. For every supplied decision topic, judge whether the rewrite preserves the mechanism the original actually advocates, its consequence, roles, timing, scope, and relevant premises. An endpoint match or shared words is insufficient. Do not repair missing or reversed reasoning. Return preserved/changed/omitted/uncertain for each decision and explain any non-preserved judgment with evidence. If a topic was absent from the original and remains absent, that may count as preserved; do not invent a missing original choice. Return an overall status of preserved/changed/uncertain and identify added conflicting decisions. No intended solution is supplied: compare only what these two texts actually say.

decision_topics.question: How should a new member learn the studio routine?
How should members obtain bench time?
How should a member prepare a project plan?
How should shared hand tools be checked out?
How should requests for project help be handled?
How should shared consumables be replenished?
How should usable offcuts enter the shared scrap supply?
How should unfinished projects be stored between sessions?
How should short noisy tasks be coordinated?
How should projects use the drying rack?
How should bench cleanup be organized?
How should a damaged tool be reported?
How should a short technique demonstration be selected?
How should personally owned surplus materials be shared?
How should members receive changes to studio routines?
How should unfinished studio duties pass between stewards?

documents.original:
At the beginning of a new member’s first visit, ask an experienced member to walk through the illustrated guide with them. The two can follow the route a project takes through the studio, with the experienced member showing how the studio works at each stop. Give the newcomer that same person’s name as someone to ask for help as the first project takes shape.

For each booking round the steward posts the order in which members may choose bench times. Rotate who goes first from round to round. Each person picks a session that suits them from the openings left, and anyone arriving can use an unclaimed session. Before going to the supply shelves, a member fills in a project card with the next task, what it will take and how far they intend to get today. Looking at the card again when they finish gives them a place to pick up next time.

Write your name against a tool’s hook number before lifting it down. Someone looking for a missing tool can go straight to its borrower, who returns it within the booked session. If it develops a fault, stop using it, put it in the marked tray and fill out a repair card with what you were doing and what you noticed. The steward can pass those observations along when getting the tool inspected. For a question about the work itself, enter it under its topic on the help list. The steward can bring people facing the same difficulty together for a short explanation while others carry on working.

Post regular, short windows for hammering and other noisy work. Members can pick an open turn at the designated station and fit quieter work around the posted times. For wet work, the maker chooses a vacant spot on the drying rack and tags the piece with their name and the earliest time it can safely be moved. Someone who will soon need rack space can see when a spot might open up.

At the end of a task, match clean, useful offcuts to the samples on the scrap shelf and put them straight into the corresponding containers. The next person can use them as soon as they’re sorted. For unfinished work, pack the piece and label it with the owner and review date, then take it to the steward. The steward chooses an open shelf position within the member’s allowance and logs the location for retrieval. Neighbors at the benches should spend their last few minutes together, doing the cleanup checklist at one bench and then the other. A second pair of eyes helps catch a tool or scrap tucked behind a project.

Each day at closing, the steward counts the common materials and brings the restock card up to date, including what is already on order. Looking over all the shortages together helps the steward decide how to spend the reorder allowance. Members with surplus materials of their own can leave the steward a labeled offer giving the amount and terms. Gather owners and prospective recipients at a weekly exchange so they can ask about the material and agree on a handover in person.

For the weekly optional demonstration, let members post techniques they would like to see and vote on the suggestions. The steward then arranges the selected lesson in the demonstration corner. When a studio routine changes, date the notice and have the steward point it out and explain it when each member next arrives. Members can ask how it affects the work they are about to do. During the overlap between stewards, have the two walk through the room together and enter outstanding duties in the handover pad as they go. The person taking over will have seen the low shelf or damaged tool behind the entry.
documents.rewrite:
Give a first-time studio member a tour as soon as they arrive. Pair them with an experienced member and have them use the pictures in the guide to trace a project’s journey around the room. At each stop the guide can show what happens there. Make sure the newcomer knows their guide’s name so they can turn to the same person as they work on their first piece.

At booking time the steward puts up a list showing whose turn it is to choose, with a different member getting first choice each round. Members go down the list, each choosing a convenient bench session from the times still free. Someone who turns up on the day can take any session nobody has claimed. Before collecting materials, fill out a card describing the next job, the supplies it needs and the stopping point you have in mind for today. Consult it again before leaving so you know where to resume.

The hook numbers double as a way of finding tools in use. Sign your name next to the number before taking the tool, and have it back before your session ends. Anyone needing it can see whom to ask. If it seems faulty, stop work with it and leave it in the designated tray. Describe the job and the symptoms on a repair card for the steward to share with whoever examines it. If you need help with a technique, write your question under the relevant heading on the help list. That lets the steward give a brief explanation to several members who need it without interrupting the rest of the room.

Schedule brief, recurring periods for loud jobs and display the times. Members can take a free turn at the station for noisy work and plan their quieter jobs around it. On the drying rack, choose an empty place yourself and mark your piece with your name and the first time it can be moved safely. Other makers can then estimate when there will be space for their own pieces.

When you finish a job, compare any clean, reusable scraps with the examples on the offcut shelf. Drop each into its matching bin so the next maker can find it immediately. Wrap up anything still in progress, add the owner’s name and the date for review, and hand it to the steward. The steward finds a vacant spot within that member’s storage allowance and records where the package went. Leave a few minutes to clean up with the person at the next bench. Run through the checklist together at each bench in turn so one of you can spot things the other might miss behind the work.

At closing every day, the steward counts shared supplies and updates the restocking card with quantities still needed and orders already placed. Seeing the shortages side by side helps with allocating the reorder budget. A member offering extra material can give the steward a labeled offer stating how much is available and on what terms. At the weekly exchange, prospective recipients can meet the owners, ask questions and arrange the transfer face to face.

Members propose and vote on techniques for the optional weekly demonstration. The steward organizes the chosen topic in the demonstration corner. Put a date on any notice changing a studio practice. The steward draws each member’s attention to it on their next visit and talks it through so they can ask about their own upcoming work. When stewards change shifts, use their time together for a circuit of the studio. Enter unfinished duties in the handover pad along the way so the incoming steward can connect an entry to the shelf that needs filling or the tool awaiting attention.

decision_topics.question: How should guests make their arrival known?
How should games enter the evening’s suggested selection?
How should guests form tables for the next games?
How should the main rules explanation be delivered?
How should players try unfamiliar actions before scored play?
How should late arrivals find a game that will start soon?
How should guests use short activities while waiting?
How should tables monitor their progress through a game?
How should a table resolve an unclear rule?
How should inexperienced players receive strategic guidance?
How should refreshments fit around games?
How should conversation volume be kept comfortable?
How should players signal a need for a personal break?
How should game components be checked after play?
How should the evening’s final stopping time be communicated?
How should guests suggest improvements for the next evening?

documents.original:
Have the host meet guests as they come in, ask their name and whether they feel like playing yet, and put both answers on the welcome sheet. That greeting gives a first-time guest someone to come back to, and the host knows who is looking for a seat. Invite people to browse the games and leave a marker by anything that catches their eye. Use the interests of the people actually in the room to make the evening’s suggestions. Other available titles can still be requested.

When there is room to start a game, willing teachers call out what they can teach. Let guests gather around, meet the teacher and ask what the game involves. The host checks that the people choosing to play fall within the player range on the box. Anyone can pass and wait for another invitation. A welcome volunteer can introduce a latecomer to a group nearly finished with its game and make a note if they agree to play the next one together. That gives the guest a group to look forward to while the current players finish. The host brings waiting guests over to a short activity already in progress and comes back to tell the group when another game can start. People can enjoy each other’s company while the host keeps track of openings.

At a new table the teacher should go over the essentials with everyone together, following the printed aid, and then invite questions about what they have just heard. Let the group call out moves to try while the teacher plays out a few turns. Seeing the suggestions in action lets everyone check their understanding together. The teacher resets the pieces before scoring starts. During the game, someone new to it can ask the teacher for advice whenever they want it. The teacher can talk through the costs and benefits apparent from the information those players can see, leaving the player to choose the move.

Write the agreed stopping time where everyone at the table can see it and choose a player to give notice as that deadline approaches. Allow time to record an unfinished position if desired and pack the box. Separately, set a timer in view of the players for checkpoints they agree on. At each ring, take a moment to see how much time remains and discuss progress. If a rule causes a dispute, the table pauses while two players spend a short time looking it up. Accept the pair’s reading, or their provisional decision for the evening if the wording remains unclear. The others need only hear the outcome, and an open question can be checked later.

A player wanting a drink or snack should agree on a brief absence with the table, use the refreshment area and come back before their next action. This accommodates individual needs and keeps the pieces dry. For a personal break, speak up before leaving and agree on a place to pause right away. Everyone should know the action to resume with, keep private information covered and wait for the player where their participation is needed. As the host goes around the room, listen for neighboring tables having trouble hearing their own play. A quiet word from the host asking a loud group to lower its voices saves the neighbors having to raise it themselves.

After each game one player reads off the contents list in order. The others collect and count the pieces into the labeled bags, with the reader checking off each group before the box goes back. The next day the host sends an optional short prompt asking about the choice of games, finding a table and any difficulty taking part. Group the replies when planning the next evening so guests have had a chance to reflect and experiences common to several different tables are easy to see.
documents.rewrite:
Greet each arrival personally. The host asks what name to put on the welcome sheet and whether the guest is ready for a game, recording that answer too. A newcomer now has a familiar face to approach, and the host can tell who needs a place. Encourage guests to look over the games and mark those they fancy. Base suggestions for the evening on the markers left by the people attending, while keeping requests open for any title available.

As space opens, people willing to teach announce their games. Give guests time to gather, talk to a teacher and find out what playing entails. Guests are free to wait for a later invitation. For those who opt in, the host checks the number against the range printed on the box. If someone comes in late, a welcome volunteer can introduce them at a table close to finishing. If they make plans to play together afterward, the volunteer notes the arrangement and the newcomer knows who they will join. Take those waiting over to a short activity underway. The host keeps an eye on available places and returns to let them know when a new game can begin.

Seat the new group together for an explanation from the teacher using the printed guide, with questions afterward. Then let everyone suggest moves and watch the teacher try them over a handful of practice turns. They can see together whether the game works as they understood it. Restore the starting position before playing for points. Once play begins, a newcomer can ask the teacher for help at any time. Using what the player can see, explain the tradeoffs and leave the choice in their hands.

Agree when the game must end and write that time in plain view. Designate someone at the table to warn the others in time to save an unfinished game if they wish and put it away. Agree on progress checks as well, using a visible timer. When it sounds, review how far the group has got and the time still available. For a disagreement over a rule, suspend play and give two players a brief chance to consult the rules. The pair report their interpretation to the table. If the text leaves them unsure, their ruling stands for the evening and the question can be researched later.

Arrange a short absence with the other players before heading to the refreshment area. Have the snack or drink there and be back for your next move, which keeps liquids away from the game. For a personal break, tell the others before stepping away and decide together on an immediate stopping point. Be clear about the action due next, conceal private information and hold any play requiring the absent person. During rounds of the room, the host listens for tables whose play is being drowned out. The host can quietly ask the louder group to bring the volume down, sparing the neighboring players that conversation.

As each game ends, have one player work down the contents list aloud. The others gather the pieces, count them and fill the marked bags while the reader ticks off each batch before returning the box. The following day, the host invites guests to answer a brief, optional follow-up about the games on offer, getting a seat and anything that made participation difficult. Guests have time to think back, and grouping their comments when organizing the next event helps the host recognize experiences shared across tables.

decision_topics.question: How should rehearsal dates be chosen from available room slots?
How should expected attendance reach the conductor?
How should singers obtain the music needed for rehearsal?
How should the order of rehearsal pieces be set?
Who should guide the shared vocal warmup?
How should chairs be arranged within voice sections?
How should short sectional practice be organized?
How should a difficult passage be diagnosed?
How should practice recordings be made easy to use?
How should singers learn shared entrances and cutoffs?
How should singers offer observations about musical balance?
How should changes to score markings be kept consistent?
How should an absent singer catch up?
How should the main rehearsal break be timed?
How should room setup duties be shared?
How should the choir agree what to practice before next time?

documents.original:
Give singers an actual draft calendar to consider. The booking organizer can lay out a series of rehearsals in slots the room has free, invite members to flag conflicts with those particular dates and make adjustments before booking. Once dates are fixed, each singer marks the shared sheet by the preceding day to say whether they expect to attend. The conductor can check the entries while deciding what will be workable with the voices due that evening.

Send everyone the numbered list of pieces and their digital scores in advance so practice can start at home. Have the corresponding paper scores ready for pickup when singers arrive. In preparing the order of work, the conductor asks each section leader where the prepared music still needs attention. Use their accounts to draw up and publish a balanced running order, giving the full choir time on passages that have been troubling particular parts.

Have a setup coordinator arrive early with the list of jobs. As volunteers turn up, the coordinator can direct one to the chairs, another to the score folders and someone else to the stand, distributing the remaining jobs to the people actually on hand. At the start of rehearsal the conductor gives a short window within which everyone can expect the main break. The conductor can stop at a suitable musical resting point inside that window, and people can still step out for personal needs.

For the familiar warmup, post the order of its approved exercises and give a different section leader responsibility for guiding each portion. Singers know who to follow through the handoffs. Have the choir sing a short phrase for the conductor to hear how the room carries the sound. On that evidence the conductor asks people to shift chairs within their own voice section, checking that each can still see the beat and that paths through the room stay clear.

Before asking the choir to sing an entrance or release together, the conductor shows the gesture and has singers put a reminder at the corresponding place in their music. It gives them something to look for as they follow the gesture in performance. Where a passage is going badly, sing it through for the conductor to identify which element is causing most of the trouble. Work on that element alone, whether it is the text, rhythm or pitches, then put the passage together again. When a section needs individual attention, the conductor takes that group. The other leaders each take their own section to a separate corner with an assigned passage. Bring everyone back together within the time allowed so the full choir benefits from the work all the groups have done.

After a combined passage the conductor can invite one section at a time to describe the balance it heard. Rotate the invitation through the parts to hear how the music sounds from different seats, then let the conductor decide what to adjust. Singers pencil in new markings as they receive them. Before people leave, the conductor reads through the affected bars aloud so singers can correct anything they heard differently. The organizer publishes the agreed changes with the piece, bar and current marking.

End rehearsal by naming two priorities for optional practice at home and putting the relevant bars in the notes. That gives singers a manageable assignment they can find again. After every session each section leader sends their own singers a short list of approved recordings in the order to practice them, with bar references to the spots that need work. Someone who missed the rehearsal receives the notes with links to the changes and the recordings. They can update their score and hear the passages on their own schedule before coming back.
documents.rewrite:
Start with the room’s available times. The organizer draws up a tentative rehearsal calendar from those openings and shows it to the singers so they can identify specific clashes. Revise the dates in light of the responses before making the bookings. For each confirmed rehearsal, ask singers to enter their expected attendance on the shared sheet by the day before. The conductor can plan for the mix of voices expected.

Circulate the pieces in a numbered list with copies of the scores in digital form so members can work on them at home. Set out matching paper copies for them to collect on arrival. Before settling the rehearsal plan, have the conductor consult the section leaders about difficulties that remain after preparation. The conductor can then publish a balanced sequence that includes time for the choir to rehearse together on the troublesome passages.

The setup coordinator should be there ahead of the singers with a list of tasks. As helpers appear, assign them to arrange seating, lay out folders, put up the stand and cover the rest of the list according to who is there. At the outset, the conductor announces a short span of time in which the main break will fall. That allows a stop at a musically convenient point and still lets singers step away separately as needed.

Display the sequence of approved exercises for the usual warmup. Assign successive portions to different section leaders so everyone knows whose direction to follow. Then listen to a brief phrase from the choir to judge the acoustics. The conductor can reposition chairs within each voice group in response, making sure every singer can see the beat and there is still a clear way through.

Demonstrate the cue for a shared entrance or cutoff before singing it. Have the singers mark the spot in their scores to remind them to watch for the gesture. If a passage is giving trouble, let the conductor hear it through and identify its main difficulty. Isolate that aspect, such as words, notes or rhythm, then sing the whole passage again. When the conductor wants to work with one section, send the others to different corners, each with its own leader and music assigned for the purpose. Reassemble within the allotted time to hear the results in the full choir.

After everyone has sung together, ask sections in turn what balance they heard. Calling on different parts in rotation gives the conductor perspectives from across the room when deciding on adjustments. Have singers pencil changes into their scores as they are given. Before dismissal, the conductor reads aloud through the bars in question so discrepancies can be corrected. The organizer circulates the agreed markings, identifying the piece and bar for each.

Close by identifying two things singers can choose to practice at home. Include the bars in the rehearsal notes so they can go straight to them. After each rehearsal the section leaders send their respective singers a short sequence of approved recordings, arranged in practice order and pointing to the bars requiring attention. Send absentees the notes along with links to both the changes and the recordings, giving them time to amend their scores and listen before they return.

decision_topics.question: How should organizers learn what neighbors expect to contribute?
How should contribution arrivals be spread across the intake period?
How should contributed goods be checked before display?
How should useful item descriptions be prepared?
How should the display tables be organized?
How should reserve stock reach the display tables?
How should arriving visitors learn how the fair works?
How should competing requests for the same item be settled?
How should claimed items be held while recipients continue browsing?
How should pieces of a complete set remain together?
How should visitors arrange help carrying goods out?
How should volunteers receive their working assignments?
How should requests for currently missing goods be recorded?
How should outgoing goods be recorded at collection?
How should unclaimed goods be processed after the fair closes?
How should organizers learn which parts of the fair need improvement?

documents.original:
Start preparations on each block by having a volunteer talk with neighbors who might bring household goods. Ask what they expect to bring and send the organizers totals by category. A conversation can reach someone who would miss a form, and the estimates help with preparation while all goods still go through the published intake checks. Invite contributors to pick a free arrival window on the intake sheet. The spaces there show when volunteers can expect a rush and let neighbors plan their trips, with a little room for walk-ins throughout. Using volunteers’ stated availability and preferences, the coordinator assigns duties and sends out the shift roster ahead of time. That gives people time to prepare and the coordinator a chance to cover gaps.

At intake, have a pair work alongside each contributor. One volunteer talks through the condition checklist while the other looks over the goods. They can ask about a loose fitting or missing part while the owner is still there. For every item accepted, the interviewer uses the owner’s answers to fill in the standard label, recording the item number, description, limitations and any accessories included. The person who heard the explanation can put it into the same fields visitors will see on other items. Record the contributor’s choice of return or donation for anything left at closing.

Mark each display table for a room of the home and group the goods by where people would ordinarily use them. A visitor furnishing a kitchen knows where to begin. Keep each complete set on a tray of its own, with one label listing its pieces. People can pick them up for a closer look and see at a glance what goes together. Keep walking aisles clear and put overflow on reserve shelves. When gaps appear on a table, its volunteer requests goods to fit them and a runner fetches suitable available pieces from reserve. This keeps the display useful as goods move out.

Let the welcome volunteer gather small groups of arrivals for a quick account of browsing, claiming an item, leaving it on hold and collecting it. Explain that taking something is free and bringing a contribution is optional. Once a group moves on, anyone wanting individual help can stay with the volunteer by the entrance diagram. Visitors seeking an item they cannot see can describe it to the request volunteer, who puts wanted types on the board and checks them against reserve goods and incoming contributions. A match can turn up even before the item reaches a table.

When several people want the same available item, record their names and request times on the sheet. At the end of its short decision window the volunteer gives it to the person whose recorded request came first. People can see how the decision was reached from the times. A recipient who wants help moving a piece can book a short carrying slot when claiming it, then bring their collection record at the agreed time to meet the helper for the trip to the pickup area.

Anyone who wants to browse a little longer can bring claimed goods to the holding volunteer. Together they establish the collection deadline, within twenty minutes. The volunteer records the recipient’s name and the deadline before shelving the goods, so both people know who is looking after them and when the recipient is due back. For collection, the recipient first shows the claim record to the recording volunteer, who verifies the claim, records the item as outgoing and checks a collection slip. The recipient presents that slip when leaving with the goods, so the record is in order before the handover at the exit.

As soon as browsing closes, sort everything unclaimed according to its contributor’s recorded choice, before admitting people for closing collection. That lets contributors find their returns and leaves the donation goods together ready for the arranged pickup afterward. Put a short optional card at the exit for visitors, contributors and volunteers alike. Asking each about finding goods, following the claim process and managing the day catches problems while people remember them and lets organizers spot difficulties mentioned by several groups.
documents.rewrite:
Ask a volunteer on each block to visit neighbors who may have household items to offer. From those conversations, report the expected quantities in each category to the organizers. This includes people who might overlook a form and gives organizers an idea of the volume to expect. Every item still needs to pass the advertised checks on arrival. Let contributors sign up for an available intake period so they can plan their trips and volunteers can anticipate busy spells. Leave some capacity for unscheduled arrivals in every period. For staffing, the coordinator takes volunteers’ preferences and available hours into account when assigning jobs. Send the roster out early enough for people to get ready and for uncovered shifts to be filled.

Meet each contributor with two volunteers. One goes over the condition questions with the owner as the other examines the goods, so questions about a missing accessory or a shaky joint can be settled on the spot. For each item that passes, the volunteer who conducted the interview transfers the answers to the usual label, entering the item number, a description, any limitations and the accessories supplied. Visitors then see each owner’s account in a consistent format. Also record whether the contributor wants unsought goods back or is happy to donate them at closing.

Organize the tables by household room and sign them accordingly, making it easy to head straight for the goods one needs. Give every complete set its own tray and a single label naming all its components so visitors can handle the pieces and still tell which belong together. Use reserve shelving for excess stock and leave the aisles open. When goods leave a display, the table volunteer asks for the kinds of items needed and a runner brings suitable replacements that are available in reserve.

The welcome volunteer takes a few new arrivals at a time through browsing, making a claim, holding goods and picking them up. Make clear that anyone can take goods free of charge and that contributions are voluntary. Once the group sets off, visitors who want more help can stay at the entrance diagram with the volunteer. Have a request volunteer take descriptions from people searching for something missing from the display. List the kinds of goods wanted on the board and look for matches among reserves and new arrivals, where an item might turn up before going on display.

For competing claims on an available piece, the volunteer enters each interested person’s name and the time they asked on the sheet. When the brief decision period ends, award the piece to the earliest recorded claimant. Anyone can check the times behind the decision. At the point of claiming, a recipient who needs a hand carrying something can reserve a short appointment. They bring their collection record to meet the helper at the appointed time for the move to the pickup area.

A recipient who wants to keep looking can take their claimed items to the volunteer responsible for holds. Agree on a pickup time no more than twenty minutes away. Before placing the goods on the shelf, the volunteer notes the recipient’s name and the deadline, making it clear who has the goods until pickup and when to return. To collect, first show the claim record to the recording volunteer. That volunteer confirms the claim, logs the departure and checks off a collection slip. Show the slip when taking the goods out so the paperwork is complete by the exit handover.

When browsing ends, use the contributors’ recorded instructions to divide the remaining goods into returns and donations before letting people in for closing collection. Contributors can locate their own goods, and the donations are together for the pickup arranged to follow. Leave an optional brief comment card at the exit for visitors, donors and volunteers. Ask how they got on with finding things, the steps for claiming them and the running of the day. Their answers capture fresh recollections and let organizers see where different groups ran into the same problem.
